text:
Community Forest Management in Zambia: Is it Working?






Community forestry
Community forest management (CFM) has emerged over the past five decades as a dominant paradigm in forest governance, grounded in the recognition that local communities — as the de facto managers over large areas of the world’s forests — are best placed to sustainably manage the resources on which they depend. At its core, CFM involves the formal transfer of management authority and resource use rights, including the right to benefit from the sale of forest resources, from state institutions to local communities (Charnley and Poe 2007; FAO 1978). Early programmes in the 1970s and 1980s focused narrowly on fuelwood supply and tree planting in South Asia and the Sahel, but CFM has since evolved into a broad and diverse set of approaches — including participatory forest management, joint forest management, and community-based forest management — implemented across Asia, Africa, Latin America and Europe (Roberts and Gautam 2003; Bray, Antinori, and Torres-Rojo 2006; Colfer and Pfund 2010; Baynes et al. 2015; Gilmour 2016).
The rationale for CFM rests on the premise that local communities, with vested interests in maintaining forest resource flows and access to place- and time-specific knowledge, can govern forests more effectively and sustainably than centralised state institutions, especially when the state has limited resources to enforce forest management regulations (Hajjar et al. 2021). Where well-implemented, CFM has delivered substantive benefits: forest regeneration (by as much as 37% in Nepal), reduced deforestation, enhanced biodiversity conservation, improved rural livelihoods and incomes, and stronger local institutions and community cohesion (Gilmour 2016; Charnley and Poe 2007; Baynes et al. 2015). Community forestry also positions local communities to participate in emerging carbon, biodiversity and ecosystem service markets, offering new revenue streams for forest protection.
Nevertheless, the outcomes of CFM globally have been mixed (Roberts and Gautam 2003). Recurring challenges include weak institutional capacity, insecure land tenure, unclear forest boundaries and competing resource claims, inequitable benefit-sharing arrangements, limited social capital, governance capacity and business acumen among local communities, and poor market access (Wily 2004; McDermott and Schreckenberg 2009). The conditions most conducive to CFM success include a sound legal framework devolving management and user rights to communities, strong government facilitation, high social capital among community members, sustained support from non-government organisations (NGOs) or private partners, effective rule enforcement, and the development of viable forest enterprises (Pagdee, Kim, and Daugherty 2006; Blomley 2013; Baynes et al. 2015). Where one or more of these conditions are absent, communities may be formally enrolled in CFM programmes without gaining meaningful authority or tangible benefits. Novel revenue streams for ecosystem services, in particular carbon, introduce a whole new set of issues, because of the heightened risks of elite capture and marginalisation of vulnerable community members, and the potentially competing interests of developers and government (Colfer, Pfund, and Sunderland 2010).


Community forestry in Zambia
In Zambia, the trajectory of CFM reflects a gradual transition across four generations of interventions (1980–2025), from early awareness campaigns and tree-planting initiatives to the large-scale adoption of formal community forestry driven largely by REDD+ and carbon finance mechanisms (Moombe, Malesu, and Harrison 2025). The context for CFM in Zambia is shaped by a distinctive land tenure situation. Although, the Lands Act (1995 amended 2015) nominally invests ownership of land in the President, 94% of the nation’s land is under customary ownership whereby significant land-use decisions reside with traditional chiefs (Sichone 2008). CFM in Zambia, therefore, involves devolution of management authority not only from the state, but also to some extent from traditional leadership. Moreover, whereas elsewhere CFM has been a critical process in promoting localised resource user rights (Bray, Antinori, and Torres-Rojo 2006), these have always been recognised under customary management in Zambia. In contrast, the shift to CFM in Zambia has been driven by a recognition at the national level of a need for sustainable forest management (SFM) to reduce deforestation and forest degradation, while promoting economic development among rural communities. The government estimates that Zambia is currently losing forests at a rate of 250,000 to 300,000 hectares annually, alongside similar amount of forest degradation (McNicol, Ryan, and Mitchard 2018), making improved forest governance through CFM a national priority aligned with the country’s nationally determined contributions (NDCs) under the Paris Agreement. Specifically, Zambia’s NDC 3.0 set a target of 8 million hectares under CFM by 2030, which by 2025 had already been substantially surpassed.
The legal and policy framework for CFM in Zambia is now well-established. The Forests Act No. 4 of 2015 and the Forests (Community Forest Management) Regulations (SI No. 11 of 2018) provide the principal legal basis for CFM, granting communities the right to apply for recognition as community forest management groups (CFMGs), prepare and implement forest management plans, and access forest user rights including rights to timber, carbon and other ecosystem service revenues.
Since the formal CFM framework came into effect, the sector has expanded rapidly. The carbon market in particular has accelerated the adoption of CFM in Zambia, offering a vehicle for partnerships between carbon developers, conservation NGOs, and local communities that benefit from forest protection (Moombe, Malesu, and Harrison 2025; Lundu, Bradley, and Ruiz-Villar 2025; Souza et al. 2026). As of March 2025, there were 351 CFMGs in Zambia, presiding over approximately 9.4 million hectares of community forests (CFs) across all ten provinces (Moombe, Malesu, and Harrison 2025). North-western Province has the largest area under CFM and Luapula the smallest. Despite this growth, implementation quality clearly varies considerably. Reflecting patterns in the global picture of CFM implementation, challenges in Zambia include inadequate exit strategies by supporting projects, inconsistent monitoring and follow-up support, low capacity in business and governance skills among CFMGs, insufficient funding to complete the formal establishment process, lack of clarity over benefit-sharing arrangements, poor representation of women despite their high dependence on NTFPs, and unresolved intra- and inter-community conflicts over land and resources (Moombe and Kaumba 2022; Lundu 2023; Souza et al. 2026).


Aims of this study
The objectives of CFM in Zambia are to improve forest management and enable sustainable local economic development. With CFM expanding rapidly in Zambia, the Government of the Republic of Zambia (GRZ), donors, and other stakeholders have recognised a critical need to understand whether CFM is achieving its intended outcomes, and where improvements in CFM implementation are required. This study was designed to fill that knowledge gap. Specifically, the study aimed to: (i) assess whether CFM in Zambia has led to improved sustainable management of forests and other natural resources; (ii) understand whether CFM has contributed to sustainable development; (iii) identify opportunities for improved implementation of CFM; and (iv) generate policy recommendations for improved CFM implementation in Zambia.
To address these aims, we surveyed 80 CFMGs across eight provinces (two provinces did not have a sufficient number of CFs to be included), combining focus group discussions (FGDs) with CFMG executives, female, male and youth community members, and individual interviews with key stakeholders, namely community members, traditional leaders, District Forestry Officers (DFOs), and representatives of private enterprises partnering with CFMGs.
To address the four aims of the study listed above, we examined CFM performance across four domains. The first and second aims are addressed through domains on SFM and economic transformation, respectively. Governance and equity & inclusion domains provide evidence on the quality of implementation and therefore also the scope for improvement. The equity & inclusion domain also helps understanding of the impact of CFM on sustainable development. Furthermore, in the last section of the interview tool, we asked stakeholders how they thought CFM was performing and how it could be improved, which provides additional information on how CFM implementation can be improved directly from the stakeholders most affected by it. To address the final aim on providing policy advice, we distilled our findings across the four domains and presented a condensed version of our findings in the Summary and Recommendations chapters that preceded this chapter.
The remainder of this report is organised as follows. The Survey Overview chapter describes the sample of community forests and interviewees. It demonstrates that the sample is sufficiently representative to support national-level inference. The Governance chapter examines whether CFMGs have completed the required legal and administrative processes, established functional governance structures, and developed business plans. The Sustainable Forest Management chapter assesses the impacts of CFM on deforestation, charcoal production, fire frequency, wildlife, and natural resource management. The Remote Sensing Analysis chapter independently examines the performance of CFM across three SFM indicators: fire incidence, tree canopy cover change and above-ground biomass change. The Economic Transformation chapter evaluates changes in access to forest resources, employment, income, and the realisation of carbon and other economic opportunities. The Equity and Inclusion chapter examines benefit sharing, gender equity, transparency, and the impacts of CFM on poverty. The Discussion chapter summarises the stakeholders’ ideas concerning the performance of CFM implementation and how it can be improved and synthesises findings across all four domains. Three appendices provide supporting material: Appendix I describes the methods in detail; Appendix II contains the full survey tool used in the FGDs and individual interviews; and Appendix III provides summary details of the 75 community forests surveyed (five CFs surveyed were defunct and so removed from the sample).

title: Sustainable Forest Management
text:
Summary
Most FGD respondents indicated that deforestation, charcoal production and fire frequency were decreasing, wildlife populations were increasing and natural resource management was improving within CFs. Most FGD groups indicated that both deforestation and charcoal production were also decreasing outside their CF, suggesting there is no leakage or a positive leakage effect. Community female FGDs tended to have a more positive view of the impact of CFM compared to the other groups, which is noteworthy given it is primarily the women who harvest forest products, but who often do not have voice in traditional natural resource management. However, it is also important to note that a small number of FGD groups and individual interviewees suggested the situation was worsening in their CFs. The Governance Index was a significant predictor of performance, according to the perceptions expressed by the FGDs. Not many CFMGs were practising restoration or establishing plantations. Existing CFs should be expanded and new ones designed so that they incorporate degraded areas that can become the focus of restoration and plantation activities and contribute to national restoration and plantation targets.






NoteKey conclusions



CFM in Zambia is demonstrably improving SFM across the large majority of surveyed communities, with positive spillover effects in the surrounding landscape and encouraging evidence of women’s engagement in forest governance. The opportunity to build on these gains through a more systematic approach to restoration and plantation is substantial and should not be deferred.

title: Sustainable Forest Management
text:
Discussion
All the indicators of SFM point to a situation that is improving under CFM, including deforestation, charcoal production, fire frequency, wildlife abundance and natural resource management. Interestingly, there does not appear to be any indication of leakage for most CFs. Most FGD groups indicated that both deforestation and charcoal production were also decreasing outside their CF. There were some differences in responses among the different FGD groups, with community female FGDs tending to have a more positive view of the impact of CFM compared to the other groups. This is interesting and may indicate that under CFM females have more of a voice in forest and forest resource management. Traditionally, women are highly dependent on forest resources, but usually have little say in forest management decisions. It would be worth following up this study to investigate what is driving this positive take on CFM among community women.
Among the individual interviewees, NGO representatives and DFOs tended to have a somewhat more conservative view with respect to positive changes, as compared to individuals from the communities. This may reflect that these professionals have a broader perspective from which to understand changes in forest and forest resource management. However, it could also arise from the fact that they are not as intimately involved in the forest management and hence less aware of the changes. Ultimately, monitoring over a longer period will enable better understanding of how CFM is changing forest management.
Overall, CFM appears to be engendering a change towards improved SFM. However, it is important to note that a small number of FGD groups and individual interviewees suggested the situation was worsening in their CFs. For the success of CFM in Zambia, it will be important to identify CFs that are doing less well, diagnose the causes and implement changes.
Some CFMGs were practicing forest restoration, mostly through protecting natural regeneration, and a few were establishing plantations. However, these activities were not widespread among CFMGs. Restoration - especially through protection of natural regeneration - should integral to CFM and could be implement across all CFs in Zambia. As this is an important indicator of SFM and there are government targets to restore 2,000,000 ha by 2030, the FD should integrate restoration targets into forest management plans for CFMGs and monitor outcomes. A problem is that the boundaries of many existing CFs were drawn around areas containing on relatively good forest. The FD and communities should consider expand CF boundaries to incorporate areas for restoration activities, and for new CFs such areas should be incorporated from the outset. Agroforestry was also not widely practised by CFMGs, but is recognised tool for restoration of degraded agricultural land and can reduce pressure on forests. Plantations are also an important opportunity for CFM. Plantations can supply local building and fuelwood needs, thereby reducing pressure on natural forests. Through sustainable charcoal programmes, they can also supply energy for urban dwellers and again reduce pressure on natural forests. Last, Zambia has an acute shortage of high quality timber for uses such as telegraph poles and construction and imports large amounts of wood. A focus on developing plantations through CFM would go some way to meeting these needs, as well as generating a valuable additional source of income for rural communities.
In conclusion, our data suggest that CFM in Zambia is driving substantial improvements in SFM, reducing deforestation, charcoal production, and fire frequency, increasing wildlife populations, and improving natural resource management. However, it is important to note that these changes were not ubiquitous across all CFs. While some CFMGs are practising restoration and establishing plantations, there is a substantial opportunity to expand the role of CFM in meeting national restoration and plantation targets.

title: Remote Sensing Analysis
text: Community Forest Management in Zambia: Is it Working?

title: Remote Sensing Analysis
text:
Summary
This chapter provides satellite-based evidence on the effects of CFM on fire, deforestation and above-ground biomass across the surveyed CFs and 1 km wide buffer zones surrounding them. Analyses used fire detection data (MODIS), tree cover loss data (Hansen Global Forest Change) and radar-based biomass estimates (Harrison et al, in prep), employing before-after models with a spatial core vs buffer control to assess leakage. Across all three fire metrics — detection density, burned area fraction and fire radiative power — there were statistically significant reductions within CF cores following establishment. Moreover, none of the fire models found any significant Before–After × Zone interaction, indicating that there was no measurable displacement of burning from CF cores into the surrounding buffer zones. According to the Hansen Global Forest Canopy dataset, tree cover loss rates within CF cores did not decrease significantly following establishment. However, the baseline deforestation rates within CF areas were already very low (median 0.14% per year), leaving limited scope for measurable decreases. There was a significant increase in tree cover loss in the 1 km buffer zones following CF establishment, but this should be interpreted with caution. The global tree cover product is known to be unreliable in miombo woodlands, where canopy cover is naturally sparse and can vary seasonally. Hence, continued monitoring over a longer period or the development of a miombo specific tree cover product are recommended before conclusions are drawn. Above-ground biomass increased significantly in both CF cores and buffer zones following CFMG establishment. For dry seasonal forests, biomass is a sensitive and ecologically meaningful indicator of forest condition, as it can detect incremental changes in tree recruitment and growth that gross deforestation metrics miss. Thus, these results support the community perspectives that forest condition is improving across a majority of CFs, as well as in their buffer zones. In contrast to the results from the survey, the governance index was not a significant predictor in models of the remote sensed data. This may reflect biases in the responses to the survey, where better or worse governance led to differing impressions of SFM performance without actually being associated with different outcomes. Alternatively, it may be that the communities are responding to small scale changes that they can appreciate, but that the signal is not yet strong enough to be detected via remote sensing. The very low levels of baseline deforestation rates within CFs raises a concern over the claims of additionality by carbon enterprises. It underlines the importance of moving from project based to jurisdictional estimates of carbon mitigation.






NoteKey conclusions



Taken together, the remote sensing evidence presents a broadly positive picture of CFM effectiveness. CFM has demonstrably reduced fire disturbance and produced measurable gains in above-ground biomass across both CF cores and 1 km buffer zones, with no evidence of displacement of pressure into surrounding areas. The possible increase in deforestation in the buffer zones warrants continued monitoring. The very low baseline deforestation rates inside CFs raises questions over the validity of additionality claims by carbon enterprises.

title: Remote Sensing Analysis
text:
Introduction
The preceding chapter examined the effects of CFM on sustainable forest management based on community perceptions collected through FGDs and individual interviews. In this chapter we provide an independent assessment of CFM impacts on SFM using satellite-derived metrics. Remote sensing offers the advantage of objective, spatially consistent measurements that are free from reporting biases, and captures processes that may be difficult for community members to perceive and quantify. However, Earth observation data have their own limitations, including the spatial grain of remote sensed productions and the fact that the remote sensing does not directly measure the processes that generate the signals.
We analysed three categories of remote sensing data. Fire dynamics were assessed using MODIS active fire detection data (Giglio, Schroeder, and Justice 2016), from which we derived three complementary metrics: fire detection density (detections per km² per year), burned area as a fraction of total zone area, and total fire radiative power (FRP) per km² — a measure of fire energy release that reflects combustion intensity and therefore the volume of biomass consumed. Deforestation was quantified using Hansen Global Forest Change 2024 tree cover loss data (Hansen et al. 2013), expressed as the annual percentage of zone area experiencing tree cover loss. Above ground biomass was assessed using a time series of 100 m resolution biomass maps from 2018-2024, generated by calibrating a generalised additive model between field plot data and radar backscatter from ALOS-2 PALSAR-2 ScanSAR (Harrison et al. in prep). Boundary data were only available for 40 out of the 75 surveyed CFs, so our remote sensing analyses were performed on this subset of the sample.
For each metric, we compared values before and after CF establishment, using the formal establishment date of each CFMG. Fire and deforestation data covered the period 2014–2024. All analyses used linear mixed models (or, for the proportional burned area response, a Gamma generalised linear mixed model with a log link), with a random intercept for CFMG to account for the non-independence of repeated annual observations within the same CF. We included the CFMG governance index as a fixed covariate to test whether governance quality moderated outcomes. To assess leakage — the displacement of forest-damaging activities into the areas surrounding CFs — we included a 1 km buffer zone around each CF as a spatial control and tested whether the Before–After change differed between core and buffer zones (i.e. the period × zone interaction). A non-significant interaction would indicate that changes in the buffer mirrored those in the CF.

title: Remote Sensing Analysis
text:
Discussion
Across all three fire metrics — detection density, burned area fraction, and fire radiative power — there were significant reductions in CF cores following establishment. These results provide robust, satellite-based confirmation that CFM has led to meaningful improvements in fire management. Importantly, in none of the fire models was the After × Buffer interaction significant, indicating that there was no measurable displacement of burning into the surrounding buffer zones. In fact, the mirrored results in the buffer zones suggests a positive leakage effect. That is, community fire management extends beyond the CF boundary. These results are consistent with the SFM chapter finding that most communities reported a reduction in fire both inside and outside their CFs.
According to the Hansen data, tree cover loss rates in CF cores did not decrease significantly following establishment. This is in contrast to the community perceptions documented in the preceding chapter and also with the results obtained for biomass which showed that biomass increased in both CF core areas and buffer zones. Several explanations for this discrepancy are possible. First, the landsat derived tree cover data are often not reliable for miombo woodlands and other savannas, where tree cover is sparse and the relative strength of the grass versus tree canopy signal can vary seasonally. Second, the median rates of tree cover loss within the CF core area varied from 0.14% before establishment to 0.13% afterwards. Thus, the deforestation rate was already low before establishment and the change is in the desirable direction, even if it was small and non significant. Meanwhile, communities may perceive improvements through indirect process-based indicators — such as reduced charcoal production or fewer incursions — that may take time to reflect in remote sensed data. The significant increase in deforestation in the buffer zones from a median of 0.26% before to 0.49% afterwards is a concern. However, as mentioned above canopy cover is not always reliably measured, especially in low tree cover environments. For example, where farmers clear scrub as part of a crop rotation cycle, it may register as tree canopy cover loss but in fact be located in previously deforested areas. Thus, this result should be interpreted with caution. We recommend tracking tree cover change over a longer period and if possible developing a miombo specific tree canopy cover product.
Currently, in seasonal dry forests biomass change is a more reliable indicator than tree cover change. However, it is also important to note that they measure different attributes. Biomass monitoring is able to detect small changes caused, for example, through the harvesting of individual trees, but tree growth and recruitment across the entire zone may cancel out small losses. Nevertheless, above-ground biomass increased significantly in CF cores and buffer zones after establishment. The biomass gain is consistent with — and may be largely attributable to — the reductions in fire disturbance documented above. Fire both kills trees directly and suppresses recruitment of woody species, so even modest reductions in annual burning can lead to measurable biomass accumulation.
The Governance Index was not a significant predictor of any outcome, in contrast to the SFM chapter where governance quality strongly predicted community perceptions of reduced fire frequency and deforestation. As discussed above, this could be because communities are focusing on process-based indicators, which may be more sensitive to governance quality. If this is the case, it may be too early to detect an effect of the governance quality in the remote sensed data. Alternative, community members may be biasing their responses based on the perception of the governance, when there is no actual real effect (or it is very weak). Indeed, both these possibilities may be true at the same time. Longer term tracking of governance and remote sensing outcomes may be necessary to resolve this.
The fact that the baseline tree canopy cover loss rate in CFs was very low calls into question the validity of addtionality claims by carbon enterprises. Given that ~80% of CFs were established for generating carbon credits, this is concerning. It underscores the necessity of moving from project based accounting to a jurisdictional approach.
Taken together, the remote sensing evidence presents a nuanced picture of CFM effectiveness in Zambia. CFM has demonstrably reduced fire disturbance and has produced measurable gains in above-ground biomass — without evidence of displacement into surrounding buffer areas. However, there has not been any measurable decrease in deforestation — as detected through the Global Forest Canopy dataset — and there is an indication that deforestation may have increased in buffer areas, although this requires further investigation.

title: Summary
text: Community Forest Management in Zambia: Is it Working?

title: Summary
text:
Survey details
Community forest management (CFM) has expanded rapidly in Zambia since receiving enabling regulations under the Forest Act in 2018. As of 2025, 351 Community Forest Management Groups (CFMGs) preside over approximately 9.4 million hectares of community forests across all ten provinces. In contrast to many other countries, CFM in Zambia involves the lawful transfer of exclusive economic rights over forest resources to CFMGs — a provision that has made Zambia an attractive destination for voluntary carbon markets and conservation investment, and has driven the rapid expansion of the programme.
This report presents findings from a survey of 80 CFMGs conducted across eight provinces in 2024. The two provinces omitted — Luapula and Copperbelt — had very few CFMGs at the time of the survey and their exclusion does not affect national representativeness. Five CFMGs included in the original sample were found to be defunct and so were excluded from further analysis, leaving a final sample of 75 CFMGs. The sample spans a wide range of CF sizes (from approximately 20 ha to over 80,000 ha) and ages (from one to approximately seven years since establishment; age distribution), and reflects the national age structure of the programme, in which most CFs are fewer than three years old.
The survey employed a multi-perspective focus group discussion (FGD) design. Four structured FGDs were conducted at each CF: with the CFMG executive committee, community men, community women and community youth (survey coverage). This design enables the systematic comparison of perspectives across stakeholder groups and is the methodological feature most critical to interpreting the equity and inclusion findings. Near-complete coverage of all four FGD types across the 75 CFs means that differences in responses among groups can be interpreted with confidence. Individual interviews were conducted with CFMG executive members, DFOs, traditional leaders, forest user-group chairs and external partners (conservation NGOs and carbon enterprises), providing an additional layer of evidence from different vantage points.
The geographic spread of the sample — covering Northwestern, Western, Lusaka, Northern, Muchinga, Eastern, Southern and Central provinces (coverage by province) — ensures that findings reflect diverse ecological, economic and socio-political contexts. The gender breakdown of interviewees is male-biased, as expected given that men dominate most CFMG stakeholder roles. However, the dedicated female FGD conducted in each CF ensured that women’s perspectives were systematically captured.
In short, the sample provides a robust, nationally representative foundation for drawing inferences about CFM implementation in Zambia. The multi-perspective design is particularly well suited to examining the equity and governance dimensions of CFM, which are among the most important — and most contested — aspects of the programme.

title: Summary
text:
Governance
The governance of CFMGs is assessed across five domains: legal processes, governance processes (elections, meetings, financial management), business processes (workplans, budgets, business plans), external support, and community buy-in. The most consistent pattern across all three process domains is that foundational steps have been taken by most CFMGs, but the more demanding ongoing requirements are frequently incomplete.
Legal processes are the most advanced domain. A large majority of CFMGs in the sample have obtained a recognition letter and signed a forest management agreement — the foundational steps for establishing a CF (legal process completion). However, later and more administratively demanding processes, including the registration certificate, forest-use permit and benefit-sharing agreement, are absent in a substantial proportion. These are not minor procedural details: without a registration certificate and forest-use permit, a CFMG’s legal basis for managing its forest and excluding external actors is weakened, and its ability to negotiate with carbon buyers and other commercial partners is compromised.
Governance processes are more unevenly implemented. Most CFMGs have held at least one election and have term limits for executive officers (election frequency), and most hold CFMG meetings with reasonable frequency. However, several basic management actions are missing in a large proportion of CFMGs: bank accounts have not been opened, receipt books are not maintained, and annual financial and technical reports are rarely produced (governance process rates). Again, these are not peripheral concerns. Without bank accounts, carbon payments and other income cannot be transparently managed. Without receipt books and financial reporting, there is no basis for demonstrating accountability to community members or to external partners. The fact that most CFMGs are overdue for elections is of particular concern. Timely elections are a basic requirement of the CFMG by-laws and overdue elections undermine democratic legitimacy. In some cases, this appears to reflect deliberate retention of control in anticipation of carbon income.
Business processes are the weakest domain. Annual workplans, budgets and business plans are present in only a minority of CFMGs (business process rates). Without these planning and financial management tools, CFMGs are poorly positioned to manage resources sustainably, account for income or sustain compliance with their forest management license.
External support presents a mixed picture. Most CFMGs are rarely or never visited by DFOs, despite the statutory duty of the FD to implement the CFM policy (DFO visit frequency). This gap is partly compensated by conservation NGOs and carbon enterprises, many of which visit their partner CFMGs regularly. However, this support is not universal: a significant proportion of CFMGs in the sample had no external partner of any kind (external partner coverage). Where NGO or carbon enterprise support is present, it has funded real improvements in forest management — patrol systems, fire management and agricultural extension. The current model, in which CFM is effectively co-governed by the community and the private sector rather than the state, may be adequate where active and capable partners are present, but leaves many CFMGs without meaningful support.
Interest in expanding the community forest, which is used as an indicator of community satisfaction with CFM, is highest among CFMG executives and lowest among community youth (interest in expansion by stakeholder group). Among individual interviewees, NGO representatives are significantly more enthusiastic about expansion than traditional leaders or community members. This divergence — consistent with the equity findings discussed below — suggests that CFMG leadership and external partners have a more optimistic assessment of CFM outcomes than the broader community. If not addressed, this gap risks eroding legitimacy and the long-term sustainability of CFM.
In summary, CFMG governance is still maturing. The legal framework for CFM is largely in place, but institutional and business management processes lag behind. Strengthening financial management, ensuring timely elections, expanding district forestry staff engagement and closing the gap between executive and community perspectives are essential to secure the future of CFM in Zambia.

title: Summary
text:
Sustainable Forest Management
Across all SFM indicators, the evidence points to meaningful improvements under CFM. Clear majorities of community FGD groups report that deforestation has decreased (reduced deforestation), charcoal production has declined, fire frequency has fallen (reduced fire) and wildlife populations have increased (wildlife recovery) within their CF. These are substantial changes in a programme that, for most communities, has been operating for fewer than five years.
Critically, the large majority of FGD groups also report that deforestation and charcoal production are decreasing in areas outside their community forest (deforestation outside CF). This is an important result, as it indicates that CFM is not simply displacing pressure from CFs into adjacent landscapes, but is generating broader environmental benefits in the surrounding area.
Community female FGD groups tend to report particularly positive changes in SFM outcomes — a pattern that recurs across multiple indicators and domains. This may reflect that women, who are traditionally highly dependent on forest resources for household provisioning but have historically had limited say in management decisions, have gained meaningful voice through CFM’s formal governance structures. Following up this finding to understand what is driving women’s positive perception of SFM outcomes would be interesting.
Among individual interviewees, DFOs and NGO representatives tend to report somewhat more conservative assessments of positive change than community members. This may reflect a broader professional perspective on forest management, or it may reflect that these professionals are less aware of the day-to-day improvements visible to those living adjacent to the CF. Longer-term monitoring will be required to disentangle these possibilities.
Restoration activities — protection of natural regeneration and, in a few cases, planting — are occurring in some CFMGs, but are not widespread (restoration uptake). Given the Zambian government’s restoration commitments and the central role that CFM could play in delivering them, this is a significant missed opportunity. A dedicated restoration component — covering natural regeneration, and planting of native and, where appropriate, exotic species — should be integrated into forest management plans for all CFMGs. Similarly, agroforestry and timber plantation establishment, which could both reduce pressure on natural forests and generate valuable additional income streams, were practised by only a small number of CFMGs.
In summary, CFM in Zambia is driving real improvements in SFM across a large majority of surveyed communities. However, these improvements are not ubiquitous. Identifying under-performing CFMGs, diagnosing the causes and implementing corrective action will be essential. Equally, integrating restoration, plantation and agroforestry components into the CFM model would substantially strengthen its contribution to national SFM targets.

title: Summary
text:
Remote Sensing analysis
The remote sensing analysis provides independent, satellite-based evidence on three key indicators of CFM effectiveness: fire incidence, deforestation rates and changes in above-ground biomass (AGB). The analysis uses a before-after design that compares outcomes within CF cores before and after establishment, and with buffer zones as a spatial control and assessment of leakage.
Across all three fire metrics — fire detection density (Figure), burned area fraction (Figure) and fire radiative power (Figure) — there were statistically significant reductions within CF cores following establishment. These results constitute robust, multi-indicator satellite confirmation that CFM has led to meaningful improvements in fire management at a landscape scale. Importantly, none of the fire models showed a significant After × Buffer interaction, indicating that fires in buffer areas had also declined. This absence of leakage from CF cores to adjacent areas is consistent with community perceptions documented in the SFM chapter, where a clear majority of FGD groups reported that fire frequency was also declining outside their CF.
According to the Hansen Global Forest Canopy dataset, tree cover loss rates within CF cores did not decrease significantly following establishment (tree cover loss). This result may initially appear contradictory given the strongly positive community perceptions, but several explanations are plausible. First, tree cover data are often unreliable at small spatial scales in miombo woodlands, where canopy cover is naturally sparse and assessments can vary seasonally due to the relative strength of the grass versus tree canopy signal. Second, baseline deforestation rates within CF cores were already very low (median of approximately 0.14% per year) before establishment, leaving limited scope for measurable further decline. The directional trend is in the right direction, even if the change is statistically modest. Meanwhile, communities may be perceiving real improvements through indirect indicators — such as reduced charcoal production, fewer incursions or recovery of the forest understorey — that are not captured by the canopy loss metric. According to the Hansen dataset there was a significant increase in tree cover loss in the 1 km buffer zones (from a median of 0.26% before CF establishment to 0.49% afterwards) around CFs. However, this should be interpreted cautiously given the measurement reliability issues noted above. Continued monitoring over a longer period or development of miombo specific tree cover analyses are recommended, before making solid conclusions.
Above-ground biomass increased significantly in both CF cores and buffer zones following CFMG establishment (above-ground biomass). For dry seasonal forests such as the miombo woodlands that dominate Zambia’s community forests, biomass is likely a more sensitive and reliable indicator of ecological condition than canopy cover loss. Biomass monitoring can detect incremental changes caused by shifts in tree recruitment and growth, which are not captured by canopy cover metrics. The observed biomass gains are consistent with — and likely substantially attributable to — the documented reductions in fire disturbance. Fire both kills trees directly and suppresses woody recruitment. Even modest reductions in annual burning can produce measurable biomass accumulation in a few years.
In summary, the remote sensing evidence presents a nuanced but largely positive picture of CFM effectiveness. CFM has demonstrably reduced fire disturbance and produced measurable gains in above-ground biomass across both CFs and in their immediate surroundings. Canopy cover was stable within CFs, but may be decreasing in the buffer areas around CFs — further monitoring of the situation is advised. The economic drivers of deforestation — charcoal production and agricultural clearance — are not directly addressed by CFM and require other interventions.

title: Summary
text:
Economic transformation
The economic outcomes of CFM are real but narrowly distributed, and the full potential remains far from being realised. The analysis covers five domains: access to forest resources, employment, carbon income, non-timber forest products and other income-generating activities, and opportunity costs.
Most FGD groups and individual interviewees indicate that CFM has not increased access to natural resources for either household use or sale. This is perhaps unsurprising, as communities were harvesting forest products before CFM was established. However, approximately one third of respondent groups felt that access had improved, likely reflecting the formalisation of community rights and establishment of user-groups.
Employment has grown under CFM (employment by FGD group), but the picture is more complicated than the headline numbers suggest. The most significant employment gains are in the roles of Honorary Forest Officers (HFOs) and community scouts — positions that are low-paying and predominantly male. Community female FGD groups were the most likely to report no change in formal employment, and community youth groups were the most likely to report gains — a difference that likely reflects the demographics of the HFO and community scout roles that CFM has generated. While new employment is a genuine achievement, the scale and quality of that employment currently falls well short of what a thriving forest-based economy should deliver.
Carbon income is the centrepiece of the CFM economic model in Zambia, and its impact is significant where it has materialised. Approximately one third of CFMG communities in the sample had received carbon payments at the time of the survey (carbon finance by province). The activities funded by carbon enterprises — patrol systems, fire management, climate-smart agriculture extension — also represent a injection of capital into forest margin communities. However, the fact that a substantial number of community youth FGD groups were unaware of carbon agreements (carbon awareness by FGD group) is concerning. It suggests that carbon enterprises may not have conducted a fully inclusive FPIC proces and that CFMG executives may not be communicating adequately with their communities. This information asymmetry is a governance risk that could erode community support for CFM over time.
Beyond carbon and honey, the economic potential of Zambia’s community forests is almost entirely untapped. A wide variety of forest products are harvested from community forests — including timber, wild fruits, medicinal plants, mushrooms, caterpillars, bamboo, resins and thatching grass — but overwhelmingly for household use or local sale with minimal value addition. Only a small number of CFMGs (15%) are partnering with any kind of enterprise (enterprise collaboration), and where they are, it is almost exclusively for honey. The communities themselves identify a rich diversity of products — prominently including timber and wild fruits as well as mushrooms and honey — that could be developed into community enterprises (unrealised opportunities). The potential to layer multiple income streams on top of one another, supply urban and regional markets with value-added products, and create more stable income for community members is substantial. CFM has the legal and institutional scaffolding to support this kind of diversified forest economy. What is lacking is the investment, technical support and market linkages needed to activate it.
Opportunity costs of CFM — foregone income, restricted access to previously used areas, time and resource costs of participation — are recognised by communities (opportunity costs by FGD group), and are important to acknowledge. Opportunity costs fall most heavily on households that were most dependent on forest clearing or other activities that are now restricted, and these households are disproportionately among the most economically vulnerable. Properly accounting for and mitigating opportunity costs — including through explicit provision in benefit-sharing arrangements and business plans — should be a standard part of CFMG management.
In summary, CFM has achieved real but limited economic transformation. The economic model currently relies too heavily on carbon and a single NTFP (honey), leaving most communities with a narrow income base that is vulnerable to market fluctuations and partner decisions. A more diversified economic model — one that exploits the full range of forest products, develops community enterprises, and actively links communities to urban, regional and international markets — is both achievable and necessary.

title: Summary
text:
Equity and Inclusion
The equity and inclusion chapter investigates a wide range of outcomes: benefit sharing, opportunity costs, gender equity, transparency, grievance and redress, and poverty impacts. The overarching finding is that equity outcomes under CFM are broadly positive, but the picture is uneven and contains important warning signals.
The most striking pattern across all equity indicators is a systematic divergence in perspective by FGD group. Community female and youth groups consistently report more negative assessments of equity outcomes than CFMG executive and community male groups — across virtually every indicator, including equitable benefit sharing (Figure), women benefiting from CFM (Figure), women’s participation in decision making (Figure), and transparency in benefit sharing (Figure). This divergence could reflect information asymmetries. CFMG executives, who are better informed about formal governance arrangements, may genuinely perceive a more equitable distribution than is visible to other community members. Alternatively — and perhaps more plausibly in some communities — it may reflect that the benefits and costs of CFM are in fact distributed unevenly, in ways that are visible to those outside the executive circle but not acknowledged by those within it. Elite capture and corruption cannot be ruled out in a subset of cases.
Notwithstanding these concerns, the overall picture is more positive than might have been expected. A clear majority of all FGD groups — including community female groups — report that benefits are being shared equitably and that women benefit from CFM. Most female groups state that women do not disproportionately bear opportunity costs, and that women participate in CFM decision making. This is an encouraging finding in a country where natural resource management has traditionally been the purview of male community members. The formal governance structures mandated by CFM — including elections, executive positions with required female representation, documented benefit-sharing arrangements, and formation of user-groups — may have given women a degree of recognition and voice that they did not previously have. In this respect, CFM may have served as a partial tool of institutional gender mainstreaming in forest management.
Community youth groups present a consistently more critical perspective across all domains. Youth are the most sceptical about CFM’s benefits, the most concerned about elite capture and transparency, and the most likely to report that CFM has not delivered meaningful livelihood improvements for their demographic. The formalisation of CFM may have worked against youth empowerment to a degree by entrenching control by older community members who dominate community management bodies, such as CFMGs. Unless addressed, youth dissatisfaction poses a genuine long-term risk to community support for CFM.
Carbon benefit-sharing agreements are structured almost entirely around revenue sharing with little provision for employment, infrastructure investment or targeted livelihood support, other than climate smart agriculture. While revenue sharing delivers a direct financial return when payments materialise, communities that have not yet received payments — which is the majority — have little tangible benefit to show. Diversifying the components of company-community agreements to include employment targets, skills development, and livelihood support would broaden both the distribution of benefits and community buy-in across diverse stakeholder groups.
The poverty impacts of CFM — primarily through increased household incomes and new income-generating activities (poverty impact) — are broadly consistent with the economic transformation findings. They are real but very limited, and the barriers that prevent the most vulnerable households from benefiting, such as low social capital and sometimes physical capacity (e.g. learning disabled or physically disabled) are structural and will require deliberate policy attention to overcome.
In summary, CFM has made meaningful progress on equity and inclusion, particularly with respect to women’s voice in forest management. However, the divergence between the perspectives of community female and youth groups on one side and CFMG executives and males on the other is the most important equity signal from this survey. Strengthening transparency, grievance and redress mechanisms, ensuring that youth groups are meaningfully engaged in benefit sharing, establishing programmes for the most vulnerable community members and monitoring for elite capture are essential to ensuring CFM delivers equitable outcomes across the full diversity of community stakeholders.

title: Policy Recommendations
text:
Community Forest Management in Zambia: Is it Working?
Derived from our findings from our research, we make the recommendations detailed below. We attempt to cover all the key changes that need to be made to improve CFM implementation in Zambia and we structure our recommendations around the same four domains that the report focuses on, namely governance, SFM, economic transformation and equity and inclusion. We acknowledge that others may have made similar recommendations and we also note that efforts may already be in place to address some of the issues. However, our purpose here is to provide a comprehensive set of recommendations that arise from our work.
Note on audience: The recommendations below are intended for three key audiences. Where relevant, we indicate the primary intended audience: [GRZ] for government policymakers and Zambia Revenue Authority, [FD] for Forestry Department managers and district-level facilitators, and [Practitioners] for NGOs, carbon enterprises, and other development partners. Many recommendations are cross-cutting and relevant to multiple audiences.

title: Policy Recommendations
text:
Governance
High quality governance is essential to CFM. The state, through the Forestry Department, must provide adequate oversight to ensure CFM regulations are being followed and the agreed upon forest management plans implemented. CFMGs must comply with their own constitutions, implement financial and management actions transparently, and ensure equitable benefit sharing, as well as functioning grievance and redress processes. Private entities, such as carbon developers and conservation NGOs, must implement FPIC processes properly and ensure their actions support CFMGs in implementing good governance.

Institutional Capacity and Oversight

[GRZ, FD] The FD should establish a national CFM unit to support implementation. This unit should focus on capacity development for forestry staff, so they are able to support CFM at the provincial and district level. In addition, forestry curricular for tertiary institutions, such as Copperbelt University and the Zambia Forestry College, need to be updated so that graduates are trained in CFM.



Monitoring and Compliance Tracking

[FD] Transition the current CFM database into a digital management dashboard for CFM monitoring that can be integrated with digital data collection tools and file uploads. Ideally, it would have an associated App that would facilitate recording of data on common processes, such as CFMG meetings and elections, permits, workplans, budgets, annual reports, and so on. The dashboard should employ a traffic light system to flag governance compliance issues, particularly: (i) timeliness and conduct of Annual General Meetings (AGMs); (ii) election frequency and term limit compliance; and (iii) expiration of executive mandates. Tracking CFM compliance is complicated and requires timely access to evidence collected through monitoring. A traffic light system will enable district staff to quickly identify CFMGs requiring prioritized support and mentoring, and will provide an objective basis for tackling elite capture through improved transparency and accountability. The Forestry Department should make maximum use of digital tools to facilitate this process.
[FD] District forest office staff should be required to visit CFMGs once per quarter and support the CFMGs in developing and implementing their budgets and workplans, as well as ensuring they are compliant with their constitutions and national regulations with respect to reporting, holding meetings and elections. They should be applying the “Checklists – CFM Step 7: Joint Monitoring, Evaluation and Lesson Learning”. CFM Step 7 serves as a critical quality assurance mechanism, verifying that CFMGs are fulfilling their obligations to protect, control access and manage their forests according to agreed management plans. Step 7 assessments also highlight gaps in earlier implementation steps (FPIC, boundary conflicts, user identification, constitution development, rules and sanctions, permits and fees). Tracking Step 7 implementation through the national database with a traffic light system will help identify mentoring needs and guide targeted support to improve CFM practice. Key Performance Indicators for district office staff should be adjusted to reflect their role in the delivery of CFM support, with quarterly CFMG visits as a measurable target.



Private Sector Engagement

[GRZ, Practitioners] Carbon developers and conservation NGOs should be required to provide support to CFMGs as a component of their business plans. The types of support should be standardised through regulations and guidelines, and should include support in CFMG governance compliance, forest management and enterprise development.



Budget and Financing

[GRZ, FD] Funds need to be made available for regular district forest office staff visits to CFMGs and for implementation of improved monitoring and compliance systems. The financial justification for this investment can be framed in several ways: (i) CFM areas function as long-term concession areas for community exclusive use, comparable to active timber concessions where the Forestry Department provides oversight—the same logic justifies investment in CFM oversight; (ii) the Forest Development Fund (established under Section 70(3) of the Forests Act, 2015) has explicit provision for promotion of community-based forest management practices, providing a potential domestic funding source; and (iii) the government’s carbon business plan should include a component for supporting improved CFMG governance as a necessary condition for realizing carbon revenues at scale. A portion of government revenue from carbon should be ear-marked specifically for CFM support, creating a dedicated funding stream.



Standardization and Transparency

[FD] The establishment of district forest enterprise officers is a step in the right direction. However, these officers also need training, so that they can support the establishment and management of community-based forest product enterprises. The Forestry Department should work in tandem with the National Forest Commodities Association to develop models for different forest product value chains.
[FD] In line with the “Checklists – CFM Step 7: Joint Monitoring, Evaluation and Lesson Learning” implementation, increased standardisation of important CFMG processes would expedite CFMG processes, simplify monitoring and reduce the risk of poor outcomes. Standardisation should cover: (i) election processes, tenure and term limits for CFMG members and executive positions; (ii) financial processes, including opening bank accounts, maintaining receipt books, payments to employees including HFOs, and gratuities to CFMG members and executives for participating in activities; (iii) reporting requirements, including presentation of annual financial and activity reports to community members; (iv) grievance and redress mechanisms; and (v) benefit sharing arrangements for both carbon and other CFMG income. A number of these are already in the standard CFM agreement, but implementation is patchy, and many could be standardised to a greater degree. Where more flexibility is required, the FD should publish guidelines, such as for different permitting arrangements and user-group management.
[FD] To improve transparency and accountability, require publishing of decisions made at CFMG meetings and posting of these around the community. Minutes of CFMG meetings should also be uploaded to the FD’s CFM database. Transparency in decision-making is a key governance marker and essential to addressing elite capture and ensuring equitable benefit sharing.
[FD] Require that the district forest office staff and CFMG executives sign off on annual budgets and workplans by a specified date and submit them to the FD CFM database. This creates accountability on both sides and ensures baseline documentation for monitoring.



User Group Registration and CFMG-Enterprise Relationship

[FD] Require registration and permitting of all forest user-groups, even if these are community groups and there is no intention to charge a permit fee. Formalising forest use and agreeing on management protocols, such as start dates and off-take levels, is essential for SFM. Community-based forest enterprises (CBFEs) should be explicitly tracked in the FD database and distinguished from the regulatory role of CFMGs.
[FD, Practitioners] Address the emerging challenge of clarifying the dual role of CFMGs as both regulators of the forest (on behalf of the whole community) and as enterprises (generating profit for shareholders/members). Where CFMGs are forced to register as Cooperatives to enable trading and bank access, legal relationships become complex and roles ambiguous. Where revenue from CFM activities goes to community social projects rather than household income, community members may lose motivation to participate and invest effort. We recommend separating these roles: CFMGs should focus on their core regulatory function—protecting, controlling access to and managing the forest according to agreed plans—while user groups and CBFEs operate as income-generating enterprises. This separation clarifies incentives, reduces role conflict, and enables the FD to better monitor CFMG compliance with forest management obligations. The relationship between CFMGs and CBFEs should be clarified in forest management plans and user group agreements.

title: Policy Recommendations
text:
Sustainable Forest Management
Sustainable forest management is one of the key objectives of CFM. Ensuring that CFMGs are taking management actions to protect and manage their forest resources is, therefore, essential. Boundary marking, patrolling by HFOs, fire prevention and other actions such as planting and restoration require annual budgets and workplans. Communities need to monitor boundary incursions and fire incidence, and track NTFP off-take, as well as record any transgressions of by-laws, such as forest clearance or tree cutting, and track the actions taken against the perpetrators, such as fines.

[FD] The district forest office staff and CFMGs should identify key SFM activities within the management plan and annual workplans and budgets — such as boundary marking, fire monitoring and patrolling — with completion dates for key milestones. These plans should be uploaded to the FD’s CFM database for monitoring. Progress on key SFM milestones should be tracked and reported through the national CFM dashboard.
[FD] Annual reports should have a standardised format that includes reporting on SFM activities, linked to key milestones set in the annual workplans. This enables comparison across CFMGs and aggregation at provincial and national levels.
[GRZ, FD] CFM is a key mechanism for the government to deliver on restoration commitments, but currently this is not being adequately implemented or assessed. CF boundaries should encompass areas that have restoration potential, such as areas that have been cleared or degraded through fire or charcoal production. The suitability of areas for restoration should also consider the ecosystem service delivery potential, such as watershed protection. CFMGs should identify restoration sites within the CF in forest management plans. Any area that is substantially degraded when the CF was established may be considered a restoration site. Within restoration sites, the management plan should identify areas for (i) natural regeneration (protection only) or (ii) planting with indigenous species or exotic species. If planting is planned, a business plan for harvesting the timber or other products should be developed to justify the decision to plant.
[FD, Practitioners] Establish community-based monitoring systems for NTFPs. The design of these systems should be standardised by the FD, so that data can be collected and aggregated at the national scale. However, monitoring should be implemented by the community using digital tools. Data should be entered into an FD-managed digital platform, with a dashboard for community viewing and district staff oversight.
[GRZ, FD] The FD should consider a small plantation programme or outgrowers schemes for CFs for timber and sustainable charcoal production. These could be established on deforested land within the CF and would contribute to Zambia’s plantation and timber production targets.

title: Policy Recommendations
text:
Economic transformation
The economic development of local communities through forest-based enterprises is, together with SFM, the other major objective of CFM. However, most forest resource use, aside from charcoal, is for household consumption or perhaps for sale through local markets with little to no value addition. Through CFM, carbon finance has brought some local investment and direct income, but the substantial opportunity for developing enterprises around other forest resources is largely going to waste. For the Zambia government to realise its ambition for economic development through CFM, a much greater investment in supporting the establishment and management of community enterprises is required.

Market Development and Knowledge Support

[GRZ, FD, Practitioners] The Forestry Department, in collaboration with the National Forest Commodities Association and other partners, should establish a national knowledge hub on forest product management, value addition, and marketing. It should help promote forest product innovation through research and technical support, and connect producers with buyers by organising forest product exhibitions at, for example, the annual agricultural shows at provincial and national levels.



Capacity Development

[FD] Provide capacity development to district forest enterprise officers. They should receive training in management and value addition for forest product value chains, business skills and financial management.
[FD] District forest enterprise officers should be required to provide capacity support for, at minimum, two forest value chains per CFMG. They should provide capacity development training for CFMG and user-group members, and support them in business management, such as in financial management and reporting. KPIs should require quarterly visits to each CFMG and documented capacity building activities.



Diversification and Market Access

[Practitioners] To address the lack of diversity in forest product economic activities, encourage carbon developers and NGOs working with CFMGs to include a minimum of two forest product value chains in each CF as a standard component of partnership agreements.
[FD] Require the production and submission to FD of business plans for CFs. These plans should be submitted alongside (or be a part of) the forest management plans that are required for CF establishment. The format should be standardised to facilitate the maintenance of quality and so that comparable data can be extracted from them.
[FD, Practitioners] Require community monitoring of harvested quantities of forest products for household use and for sale, using digital tools as described in the SFM section above. Data should be aggregated to assess sustainability of off-take levels and to identify emerging economic opportunities.
[FD] Require recording of employment statistics, such as types of jobs and hours worked per month, as a component of the community monitoring. This will enable tracking of employment creation and identification of opportunities to improve job quality.
[GRZ, FD, Practitioners] Develop a programme for community-based eco-tourism through CFs and their intersection with national heritage sites. This should build on experiences at existing sites, such as M’panshya Campsite, Rufunsa.



Forest Certification and Performance Standards

[FD, Practitioners] Consider promoting Forest Stewardship Certification (FSC) for CFMGs, but with realistic expectations. FSC certification can improve carbon credit values and open international markets for NTFPs. However, transaction costs for individual CFMG certification can be high. The value of FSC depends on whether CFMGs can access premium markets. Practitioners should conduct market analysis to assess whether the Zambian timber export market is sufficiently developed to absorb FSC-certified products and whether transaction costs can be recovered through price premiums. A group certification approach may be more cost-effective than individual CFMG certification. Any FSC initiative should be paired with capacity building to ensure CFMGs can meet certification requirements.
[GRZ, FD] Develop explicit performance standards for CFM implementation. While national guidelines provide recommended processes and expected outputs, formal performance standards should be established to enable monitoring of CFMG capacity and service provider performance. These standards should cover: (i) governance processes (elections, meetings, financial management); (ii) forest management actions (boundary maintenance, patrols, fire prevention); (iii) sustainable harvest of forest products; and (iv) benefit sharing and equity outcomes. Reference the example of performance standards developed for Participatory Forestry in Malawi, which enabled consistent monitoring across multiple CF service providers and projects. Performance standards should be integrated into the monitoring dashboard and used to guide capacity building and support.

title: Policy Recommendations
text:
Equity and inclusion
Equity and inclusion is a critical component of the social and economic development that should be achieved through CFM. First, the democratic processes involved in CFM, such as representation through the CFMG and participation in forest user-groups, give a voice to community members who might otherwise not be heard. Specific stipulations in the CFMG constitution can promote this further by requiring, for example, women or youth representatives on the CFMG and its executive. Second, forest resources often provide a safety-net for vulnerable community members, for example, by providing food resources at times of year when they experience seasonal hunger. Again, through representation, CFM can ensure these resources and the access rights of vulnerable community members are protected and also provide opportunities for vulnerable community members to participate in forest resource-based enterprises. However, with poor governance there are risks of elite capture and further marginalisation of vulnerable community members by excluding them from accessing essential forest resources. Hence, oversight of equity and exclusion provisions and their implementation is essential.

[FD, Practitioners] Require identification of opportunity costs of CFM and the community members most negatively affected in the forest management plan, and require a mitigation plan for the impacts of these opportunity costs. This should be a specific component of the forest management plan and monitored through the national CFM database.
[FD, Practitioners] Require consideration of vulnerable groups in the designation of forest user-groups and in the benefit-sharing arrangements. User-group formation should explicitly address participation by vulnerable households, including the elderly, people with disabilities, and those with limited social capital.
[FD, Practitioners] Encourage and support development of women’s and youth forest product enterprises. These could be supported through dedicated funding, capacity building, and market linkages to ensure that benefits from CFM reach beyond traditional powerholders.

title: Discussion
text:
Summary
CFM in Zambia is broadly working but there is significant room for improvement. On the positive side, a clear majority of communities report that CFM has reduced deforestation, lowered fire frequency, and increased wildlife populations — the core indicators of SFM. Most communities also recognise livelihood gains from increased employment and income, and enumerator observations confirm that many CFMGs are actively engaged and functioning.
However, governance remains a critical weakness. Many CFMGs have not completed basic legal and administrative processes, financial management processes are often absent, and DFO oversight is infrequent despite the statutory role of the FD. A number of CFMGs are dormant or struggling, and community feedback is highlights many failings, especially around transparency and benefit sharing. The enumerator observations, which flagged capacity gaps, re-engagement needs, dormant CFMGs, leadership challenges, and elite capture, paint a picture of CFM implementation that is on the verge of failing in a significant minority of cases.
Economic transformation is limited and over-reliant on a single revenue stream, namely carbon. At the time of the survey, on around one third of CFMGs had received carbon payments. Honey was the only other forest commodity that was being widely exploited, but only by about 20% of CFMGs. The broader potential of forest product enterprises — documented across a wide diversity of NTFPs — remains largely untapped.
Equity outcomes are broadly positive, with CFM appearing to give women a formal voice in forest management they often lacked before. However, youth marginalisation and elite capture are visible in a minority of CFMGs and must be actively identified and addressed.
Communities themselves have a clear understanding of what is and is not working, and their feedback on training needs, monitoring approaches, and areas for improvement, as documented in this chapter, provides a practical roadmap for strengthening CFM across Zambia.






NoteKey conclusions



CFM has clearly led to a number of positive outcomes for SFM and livelihoods. Through formalising local management it has enabled investment in forest management from conservation NGOs and carbon enterprises. However, there is a substantial concern around the FD’s capacity to provide the necessary oversight and support for CFM. The FD should invest in digital support tools for management of CMF, support DFOs to visit CFs regularly and provide training on CFM to forestry staff. Furthermore, the government of Zambia and private entities supporting CFM should support CFMGs to diversify forest product enterprises, increase value addition and enhance market linkages. CFM represents a significant opportunity for both improving SFM and realising economic transformation of rural communities, but it is likely to fall well short of its potential if these governance and economic development issues are not addressed.

Feedback from the communities

What is working in CFM
We asked the community FGD groups to identify aspects of CFM that they feel are working well in their communities (Figure 1). The most frequently mentioned reflect different aspects of SFM. Clearly, most communities do feel that CFM has led to improvements in forest management, reducing deforestation and enhancing wildlife conservation. Also mentioned, but less frequently, were indicators of good governance and improved livelihoods. Evidently, CFM is working well for some communities.

Monitoring methods
We asked the FGD groups to identify the methods they recommend are used to monitor CFM progress and outcomes in their communities (Figure 4). While a large number of approaches were mentioned, the community groups overwhelmingly identified community meetings and field visits/patrols as being the preferred approaches for monitoring CFM outcomes. Comments from the enumerators
